newsitem.title: USA: Small rate rise won't hit economy much - US official.
newsitem.headline: Small rate rise won't hit economy much - US official.

text.p: A senior administration official on Thursday forecast a continuing expansion for the U.S. economy and said a small rise in interest rates would not knock it off course.
"I don't think the economy is poised on the precipice of recession or of very slow growth," Commerce Undersecretary Everett Ehrlich told Reuters Financial Television.
"I don't think that small changes in interest rates around the margins would change that character," he added.
Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan Wednesday hinted of the possibility of higher interest rates in the future.
"I don't see why this expansion can't continue for some while," Ehrlich said, noting that inflation is "very benign."

While acknowledging that there was some "small" evidence that the strong dollar is starting to hurt U.S. exports, Ehrlich argued that its overall economic impact was positive by helping to keeping inflation down.

"There is evidence that exchange rates are beginning to work themselves into our trade flows," he said. "Even if that is the case, we to have to recognize that the dollar's role in disciplining the final price level of the United States brings very broad benefits that are good for everybody."
"I think that exchange rates are a positive in the economy right now," Ehrlich added.

He declined comment on the steep drop in stock and bond markets on Wednesday in response to Greenspan's comments. Besides hinting at a possible interest rate rise, Greenspan also warned that U.S. stock prices may have risen too far.

Ehrlich though did say he was optimistic about the outlook for corporate profits, thanks partly to what he called "right-sizing", as opposed to downsizing, by U.S. companies. "It leaves me somewhat optimistic about the prospects for profit growth as we go into the next several years," he said.
Ehrlich said that the prospects for industrial production are good as there is no overhang of inventories.

"I don't think that we're going to see a significant overhang of inventories in the next several quarters," he added, explaining, "There's better management, more effective management (of inventories)."
